A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ShortcutsBench and provide readable, directly matchable text, equations, figures and tables. v1 ends with references despite mentioning an appendix; v3 includes Appendix A.1–A.9. The comparison includes all supplied material and distinguishes newly documented procedures from demonstrated procedural changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine LLM-based agents, including API selection, parameter filling and input-need recognition results in Figures 3–6 and Table 3.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds GPT-4o-mini results, evaluations on existing benchmarks, query-quality validation, and comparisons of specialized models with their base models.

M1.justification: Both versions construct the benchmark from Apple Shortcuts, generate queries with GPT-4o, and evaluate adapted ReAct agents using correct historical actions. v3 expands collection, validation and prompt documentation without establishing a changed proposed agent algorithm, architecture or objective.

E1.justification: v3 Table 1 adds actual API-selection evaluations on MetaTool, ToolLLM and ToolBench, which v1 only discussed as existing resources. ShortcutsBench's Apple ecosystem coverage, eight task categories and three principal evaluation tasks remain.

E2.justification: GPT-4o-mini joins the nine retained agents in the main comparisons. Appendix A.9 additionally evaluates six specialized models from AgentLM, xLAM and Lemur against five LLaMA-2, Mistral and Mixtral base models. Table 1 also introduces comparisons involving smaller LLaMA and Qwen models.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce substantial evaluation settings: a human assessment of queries generated by three LLMs on 100 samples, and specialized-model comparisons restricted to three difficulty levels with 4k/32k contexts and GPT-4o-mini output conversion followed by manual verification. The main evaluation's 5,220-query grouping and accuracy metrics remain; newly disclosed existing test coverage does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: v3 adds a query-quality audit and paired base-versus-fine-tuned comparisons testing whether specialization improves the three evaluated abilities. It also adds quantified cost analysis. These substantially extend the retained difficulty, task-category and output-error analyses.

E5.justification: v3 Table 2 newly marks ToolQA's average API and action counts as estimates. Otherwise statistical reporting remains similar: Figures 4–5 retain descriptive boxplots and means/standard deviations, and neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds cross-benchmark scores, the 94/100 query-quality result, specialized-model results in Table 7, and GPT-4o-mini results, including 36.71% overall input-need recognition. The original nine agents' parameter-filling and recognition values are retained. Reported dataset summaries also change, including 7,628 to 7,627 shortcuts and overall evaluation action length from 7.48 to 8.34.

T1.justification: The mathematical task definitions, candidate-API augmentation formula and accuracy formulas are retained. Appendix explanations introduce no new theorem, proof, substantive derivation or formal assumption.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and three evaluated abilities remain unchanged. v3 extends the benchmark-discrimination claim explicitly to models as small as 3B and qualifies the introduction's open-versus-closed model parity claim to simpler tasks, aligning it with the qualification already present in v1's results.

C2.justification: Appendix A.9 adds interpretations about API-specific versus code-oriented fine-tuning, context-length weaknesses and the need to train input-need recognition explicitly. v3 also discusses imperfect generated queries, omitted models and cost-effectiveness. Some new interpretations overreach: A.9.3 calls xLAM-8x7b-r less accurate than xLAM-7b-r although Table 7 places it higher in two of three API-selection rows.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1–A.7 supplies source-site counts, acquisition and validation procedures, collection times, API-format examples, and complete generation, classification and agent prompts absent from the supplied v1. Table 6 newly discloses costs and model-specific testing coverage, including approximately 800 Gemini-Pro instances. The release statement changes from promised availability to reported availability of datasets, code, logs and results.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands to specialized agent tuning through AgentTuning/AgentLM and xLAM, with substantive discussion of their transfer limitations. Related work also adds code-agent research and benchmarks such as ANPL, AgentCoder, CodeAct, AppWorld and AgentBench; the resource comparison adds ToolLens. These extend coverage beyond bibliographic publication updates.

P1.justification: v3 substantially revises the introduction and contribution list, rewrites parts of related work and acquisition, and expands explanations of existing procedures into organized appendix sections. Specific appendix references replace v1's unsupported generic pointers. The main section order remains, but explanatory coverage and narrative structure change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, existing result plots are resized and expanded for another model, and Figure 5 changes its color scheme. Four new tables and Figures 7–13 add benchmark comparisons, acquisition and cost information, fine-tuning results, examples and prompt displays. These are substantial display additions beyond renumbering the retained tables.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially remedies v1's missing reproducibility material by supplying complete prompts, processing explanations and actual testing coverage. Cross-benchmark experiments, query-quality validation and base-versus-fine-tuned comparisons also broaden empirical scrutiny. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems: the revised Table 3 overall averages do not reconcile with its subgroup statistics, Table 6 conflicts with the cost discussion, and some Appendix A.9 interpretations overstate Table 7. The improvement rests on better documentation and evidence, rather than higher retained-model scores.
